abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Insecticides are one of the many factors contributing to the decline of pollinator populations. Agricultural pests, such as aphids and Lepidoptera, have developed widespread resistance to a large number of compounds. However, research on insecticide resistance in pollinators is rather limited and has mainly focused on metabolic resistance. To address this knowledge gap, 4897 publicly available Apis mellifera whole genomes were screened for mutations in the exons of 17 insecticide target site genes and four housekeeping genes. These genomes originated from 54 countries and cover more than 20 A. mellifera subspecies and populations. A total of 5269 synonymous and 4465 non-synonymous mutations were identified. These mutations show differing geographical and functional patterns of diversity. While the majority of mutations were classified as rare or could not be directly linked to insecticide resistance, several candidate resistance variants were identified. Furthermore, mutations previously associated with local adaptation are described. This study provides a foundation for further research on insecticide resistance and local adaptation in pollinators.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), 3.45 million tonnes of pesticides were used worldwide in 2020 [1]. Twenty-two percent of these pesticides were insecticides, which were used to combat agricultural pests such as aphids, caterpillars, planthoppers, and locusts, or to limit the spread of disease-carrying mosquitoes [2]. However, these insecticides affect not only their target species but also non-target species, such as pollinators, which inadvertently encounter them while foraging or inside the hive. Furthermore, pyrethroid, organophosphate and formamidine acaricides are used to treat honey bee colonies against Varroa destructor [3–5]. Over 100 different pesticides and pesticide derivatives have been found in honey bee colonies [3–5]. It has been observed that 86% of all worker bee samples and 99% of all wax and pollen samples contained at least one pesticide [3–5]. Insecticides and other pesticides have lethal and sub-lethal effects that impact all aspects of honey bee physiology, including development, learning behaviour, fertility, immunity, and thermoregulation [6–12]. The majority of wild plants and a third of global agricultural production depend on pollinators for reproduction [13–15]. However, pollinator populations are declining due to habitat loss, climate change, parasites, diseases, and pesticides [13, 16, 17]. Sanchez-Bayo and Goka [18] estimated that neonicotinoid insecticides pose the highest risk for honey bees, followed by pyrethroids, carbamates, and pyrazoles based on their toxicity, prevalence, and concentration within the hive.

Over 600 mite and insect species have developed resistance to at least one insecticide [19]. Insecticide resistance can arise through multiple pathways. Penetration resistance occurs through alterations in the external cuticle, thereby preventing the penetration and uptake of insecticides [20, 21]. Sequestration resistance is mediated by changes in olfactory proteins that bind the insecticide, thereby preventing it from binding its target site(s) [21]. Metabolic resistance is caused by genetic variation in the function and expression of detoxification genes. The major detoxification gene families are the cytochrome P450s, glutathione-S-transferases, glucuronosyltransferases, carboxylesterases, and ABC transporters [20, 21]. Target-site resistance is caused by mutations in the genes encoding the specific targets of the pesticides. These mutations alter the binding of the insecticide to the target site, thereby reducing the efficacy of the insecticide. Target-site resistance mutations have been described in a wide range of agricultural pests [19, 22–37]. In certain cases, these mutations have a fitness cost as they also affect the primary function of those genes [27, 36, 38–43].

Interestingly, insecticide sensitivity varies both between Apis species and among Apis mellifera subspecies. The eastern honey bee, Apis cerana, seems to be more resistant to most neonicotinoids than the western honey bee, A. mellifera [44]. Conversely, A. mellifera is more resistant to pyrethroids and organophosphates than A. cerana [45]. Moreover, there are differences in insecticide resistance among the different subspecies of A. mellifera. For example, in the United States, A. m. ligustica and the Pol-line population are significantly more sensitive to pesticides than A. m. carnica and feral populations [46, 47]. More specifically, A. m. carnica is 34 times more resistant to the neonicotinoid imidacloprid than A. m. ligustica [47]. Furthermore, the European stock of A. m. carnica is more resistant to a mix of pesticides than the North American stock of A. m. carnica [46]. Additionally, honey bees of European descent seem to be more resistant to pyrethroids than Africanized honey bees [48]. Variation in neonicotinoid resistance has also been observed between colonies of the same subspecies [49]. Tsvetkov et al. [49] estimated the heritability of clothianidin resistance at 37.8%. Some of this variability in insecticide resistance is attributed to mutations in detoxification genes such as cytochrome P450s or carboxylesterases [46, 49]. However, there is no information on the genetic variability of insecticide target sites in A. mellifera. Therefore, we investigated the diversity of mutations in seven insecticide target sites, covering 17 genes, using 4,897 publicly available A. mellifera genomes, covering a wide geographical range ([50–64], S59). The seven studied target sites are the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR), the voltage-gated sodium (NaV) channel, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) gated chloride channel subunit Rdl, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluCl), the octopamine receptor β2 and the acetylcholine esterase 2 (AChE2). These target sites cover the most frequently used insecticides and miticides in agriculture and apiculture [12, 23, 26, 29, 34, 35, 65–71]. This study aimed to examine the natural diversity of insecticide target sites and assess whether candidate resistance variants occur in geographic regions or evolutionary lineages historically exposed to insecticides.

sec.title: Abundance of rare non-synonymous mutations in insecticide target genes
sec.p: We screened 4897 publicly available A. mellifera genomes and uncovered a total of 5269 synonymous and 4465 non-synonymous mutations in the exons of 17 insecticide target site genes and four housekeeping genes (Table 1, Table S1). Of all 4465 non-synonymous mutations, 4308 (96.48%) were classified as rare. A mutation was classified as non-rare if the variant allele frequency (VAF) was higher than or equal to 5% and the variant allele count (VAC) exceeded 2 in at least one country or population [72]. The VAC threshold helped reduce false positives in countries or populations with low sample sizes. Overall, we identified 157 non-rare mutations (3.52%) (Table 1). The ryanodine receptor (15,499 bp), the octopamine receptor β2 (1441 bp), and acetylcholine esterase 2 (1790 bp) had the highest number of non-rare mutations—28, 23 and 19, respectively (Table 1). Furthermore, the ryanodine receptor, the octopamine receptor β2, and nAChRα5 had the highest number of non-rare mutations with FST above 0.9 (Table 1).

sec.title: Previously reported insecticide resistance mutations from other species are rare
sec.p: Twenty-seven mutations were identified at positions previously associated with insecticide resistance in other species (Table 2). Two of these are identical to known insecticide resistance mutations: a tyrosine to histidine substitution at position 235 of the octopamine receptor β2 and an isoleucine to valine substitution at position 1770 of the sodium channel. Both mutations have been detected in amitraz and pyrethroid-resistant populations of V. destructor (Table 2). All 27 mutations were classified as rare mutations (Table 2).

sec.title: Non-rare mutations vary strongly across regions and populations
sec.p: The highest number of non-rare mutations was found in South America and Algeria, while Turkey, Austria, Syria, and Saudi Arabia had the lowest (Fig. 1). South America had significantly more non-rare mutations than Europe, Africa, and Asia (Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05; Table 3). On the other hand, the UK, the Iberian Peninsula, Switzerland, New Caledonia, and Algeria had the highest number of variant alleles per sample among non-rare mutations, while Scandinavian countries had the lowest number (Fig. 2). A. m. intermissa, A. m. scutellata, and A. m. capensis had the highest number of non-rare mutations, while A. m. anatoliaca, A. m. syriaca, and the artificial breed Buckfast had the lowest (Fig. 3). Finally, A. m. iberiensis, A. m. intermissa, and A. m. sahariensis had the highest number of variant alleles per sample among non-rare mutations, while A. m. caucasia, Buckfast, and the Chinese Dongbei population had the lowest (Fig. 4). Ethiopia, Madagascar, Burkina Faso, and Portugal had the highest number of non-rare mutations with FST above 0.9 (S61). Conversely, no non-rare mutations with FST above 0.9 were found in Canada, China, Colombia, South Africa, Germany and Poland (S61).

sec.title: Glutamate receptor variation mirrors housekeeping genes
sec.p: The glutamate receptor carried a similar number of non-synonymous mutations per base pair and variant alleles per mutation as the housekeeping genes RpL32, RpL8, and actin (Fig. 5). No non-rare mutations were identified in this gene (Table 1). The average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 had a significant effect (ANOVA, df(1,27), p = 0.0098) on the number of variant alleles per sample in this receptor (Table 3).

sec.title: Sodium channel para shows limited non-rare variation
sec.p: The sodium channel para had a comparable number of non-synonymous mutations per base pair and variant alleles per mutation as the housekeeping genes RpL8 and actin (Fig. 5). One non-rare mutation was identified in Ethiopia with a VAF of 21,43% (Tables 1, S1). The average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 did not have a significant (ANOVA, df(1,27), p = 0.6647) effect on the number of variant alleles per sample, but the continent did have a significant effect (ANOVA, df(5,27), p = 0.0477, Table 3). No significant pairwise comparisons between continents were identified (Table 3). The number of variant alleles per sample was highest in Ethiopia and Argentina, as well as in A. m. monticola, A. m. unicolor, and North American feral populations (Figs. S4, S5).

sec.title: Limited non-rare variation in the GABA receptor Rdl
sec.p: The GABA receptor Rdl had a comparable number of non-synonymous mutations and variant alleles per mutation as the housekeeping genes RpL32, RpL8, and actin (Fig. 5). Four non-rare mutations were identified (Tables 1, S1). Neither the average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 nor the continent had a significant effect on the number of variant alleles per sample (ANOVA, df(1,27) & df (5,27), p = 0.1847 and 0.4408, Table 3). The number of variant alleles per sample was highest in Argentina and Portugal, as well as in A. m. iberiensis and A. m. capensis/A. m. scutellata subspecies (Figs. S6, S7).

sec.title: Higher non-synonymous mutation density in the ryanodine receptor
sec.p: The ryanodine receptor had a comparable number of variant alleles per but a higher number of non-synonymous mutations per base pair compared to the housekeeping genes RpL32, RpL8, and actin (Fig. 5). Twenty-eight non-rare mutations were identified (Tables 1, S1). Neither the average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 nor the continent had a significant (ANOVA, df(1,27) & df (5,27), p = 0.4320 and 0.2694, respectively) effect on the number of variant alleles per sample (Table 3). The highest number of variant alleles per sample was observed in Argentina as well as in A. m. unicolor, A. m. iberiensis, A. m. pomonella, and North American feral populations (Figs. S8, S9). The non-rare mutations showed a high number of variant alleles per sample in the Iberian Peninsula, the UK and Oceania (Figs. S10, S11). Brazil and Sweden, as well as A. m. ligustica, had the highest number of non-rare mutations (Figs. S12, S13).

sec.title: nAChR subunits show heterogeneous patterns of genetic variation
sec.p: The eleven nAChR subunits exhibited variable patterns of genetic diversity, both functionally and geographically (Figs. 5, S14-41; Table 4). The continent had a significant effect on the number of variant alleles per sample in the α3 and α4 subunits (ANOVA, df(1,27) & df (5,27), p = 0.0004 and p < 0.0001, respectively, Table 3). In these subunits, African countries were significantly more diverse than European and North American countries (Table 3). The α2, α6, and α7 subunits varied mainly in the N-terminal domain compared to the housekeeping genes (Table 4). The majority of the genetic variation in the α1 and α3 subunits was located in the linkers between the different (sub)domains. The α4 subunit varied mainly in the ligand-binding domain. Finally, the α5, α8, and β2 subunits differed from the housekeeping genes in multiple functional domains.

sec.title: Acetylcholine esterase 2 harbours multiple non-rare mutations
sec.p: The number of non-synonymous mutations per base pair and variant alleles per mutation found in acetylcholine esterase 2 differed from the housekeeping genes (Fig. 5). Nineteen non-rare mutations were identified (Tables 1, S1). Neither the average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 nor the continent had a significant effect on the number of variant alleles per sample (ANOVA, df(1,27) & df (5,27), p = 0.6512 and p = 0.2073 respectively, Table 3). The highest numbers of variant alleles per sample were observed in Argentina, Syria, Saudi Arabia, as well as in A. m. capensis/A. m. scutellata and A. m. syriaca (Figs. S42, S43). The non-rare mutations had a high number of variant alleles per sample in Syria, Saudi Arabia, and the USA, as well as in A. m. syriaca and A. m. capensis/A. m. scutellata (Figs. S44, S45). Algeria, Mexico, and the Koehnen stock had the highest number of non-rare mutations (Figs. S46, S47).

sec.title: Octopamine receptor β2 shows the highest level of coding variation
sec.p: The number of non-synonymous mutations per base pair and variant alleles per mutation found in the octopamine receptor β2 differed the most among all target sites compared to the housekeeping genes (Fig. 5). Twenty-three non-rare mutations were identified (Tables 1, S1). Ten of these were located in the shared domain of the octopamine receptor (Table S1), while 13 were located in the splicing-specific C-terminal domain, resulting in 12 variant isoforms (Table S50). Non-rare mutations in the shared domain were nearly absent in North America, Europe and Asia, and were primarily found in South America and Africa (Figs. S51-54). Non-rare mutations in the C-terminal domain were most diverse in Kenya and in A. m. monticola and A. m. scutellata (Figs. S55-S58). Additionally, South American countries had a high number of non-rare mutations in this domain, while the UK had a high number of variant alleles per sample (Figs. S55-S58). The average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 did not have a significant effect on the number of variant alleles per sample (ANOVA, df(1,27) & df(5,27), p = 0.7225, Table 3). However, the continent had a significant effect (ANOVA, p = 0.0012), with African countries showing significantly more variant alleles per sample than European and Asian countries (Tukey's HSD, p = 0.0007 and p = 0.0308, respectively, Table 3).

sec.title: Patterns of Tajima's D and nucleotide diversity across genes and geographic regions
sec.p: All Tajima's D values were within the −2 to 2 interval, a commonly used heuristic for identifying extreme deviations from neutrality (S60,S62). The largest deviations from zero were observed in Sweden: −0.72 in nAChRα8 and 1.14 in actin (S60,S62). The Tajima's D of the housekeeping gene RpL32 was significantly lower than all insecticide target site genes (Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05) (S62). No significant differences were observed between insecticide target sites (S60,S62). Argentina, Austria, China, Italy, Kenya, Madagascar, Morocco, and Poland differed significantly from the average reference (p < 0.05, relative to the overall mean) (S60,S63).

Nucleotide diversity (π) varied significantly among genes and countries. Gene and country had a significant effect on nucleotide diversity (ANOVA, df(20,27), p < 0.05) (S60,S64). Several countries exhibited significantly higher average π than the global mean, most notably Brazil, Algeria, Kenya, Morocco, Colombia, and Ethiopia, whereas Finland, Italy, Slovenia, Sweden, Portugal, and Germany showed significantly lower π values (p < 0.05, relative to the overall mean). At the gene level, π differed markedly among loci when averaged across countries. The highest π was observed in nAChRα2, RyR, AchE2, and nAChRβ1, whereas housekeeping genes such as RpL32, RpL8, Actin, and GAPDH displayed significantly reduced diversity (p < 0.05, relative to the overall mean) (S60,S64).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We found substantial heterogeneity in rare mutations within the insecticide target sites of A. mellifera. Twenty-five mutations were observed at the same amino acid position as previously described insecticide resistance mutations in other insects and two were exact matches to known insecticide resistance mutations in V. destructor [22, 23, 26, 28–31, 35–38, 41, 73]. However, none of these mutations had a VAF higher than 5%. Therefore, the insecticide resistance mutations reported in the literature appear to be rare or absent in A. mellifera and may only occur at low frequency in certain populations.

We found no significant effect of the average pesticide use per hectare between 1990 and 2021 on the genetic diversity of insecticide target sites, except for the glutamate receptor. However, this significant effect is likely spurious since all mutations in this receptor are rare. One possibility is that insecticide resistance mutations do not exist in A. mellifera, which is strengthened by the lack of extreme deviations from neutrality in the Tajima's D values. However, as we will discuss later, several candidate insecticide resistance variants are present in our dataset. An alternative explanation is that the pesticide use per hectare data are too coarse, as they include herbicides, fungicides, and all types of insecticides. As a result, the dataset lacks the resolution needed to assess the impact of specific insecticides on target sites. The PEST-CHEMGRIDS database developed by Maggi et al. (2019) has potential for the resolution needed. However, currently this database only contains information on a handful of insecticides [74, 75].

The glutamate receptor had a similar number of mutations per amino acid and variant alleles per mutation as three of the housekeeping genes. No mutations with a VAF higher than 5% were detected. Therefore, we can conclude that this receptor is highly conserved in A. mellifera and that the presence of insecticide resistance mutations in this receptor is unlikely.

The sodium channel para had a similar number of mutations per amino acid and variant alleles per mutation as the housekeeping genes indicating that this gene is also highly conserved in A. mellifera. Only one non-rare mutation was identified, a glycine-to-serine substitution found in Ethiopia, with a VAF of 21,43%. This mutation also had an FST higher than 0.9 in Ethiopia. This mutation is located in a linker within the first transmembrane domain, where no pyrethroid resistance mutations have been described so far [22, 23]. Furthermore, Ethiopia did not differ significantly from the average reference in the Tajima´s D and nucleotide diversity for this gene. On the other hand, more than 100 rare mutations were identified in pyrethroid resistance-associated functional regions described in other insects [22, 23]. Thus, significant target-site pyrethroid resistance in A. mellifera is in all probability rare, but our data shows that candidate pyrethroid resistance mutations exist. Therefore, the described differences in pyrethroid sensitivity between European and Africanized bees (A. m. scutellata) and between three North American commercial strains are presumably caused by other types of insecticide resistance such as metabolic resistance [47, 48].

Based on our data, the GABA receptor Rdl appears to be relatively conserved. While four non-rare mutations were identified, only one was located in an insecticide binding domain [31, 32]. This mutation creates a premature stop codon in the first transmembrane domain. It was found in Portugal with a VAF of 5.77%. This nonsense mutation has a high potential for insecticide resistance as it probably produces a truncated, non-functional protein thereby preventing insecticides from binding. Its low prevalence may be due to a recent origin of the mutation, low selective pressure, or the fitness costs associated with the mutation [27, 36, 38–43]. Given the low number of observed variants, this mutation should be interpreted with caution, as it may be influenced by technical artefacts. Three additional missense mutations were found in the intracellular loop between the third and fourth transmembrane domains. The effect of these mutations on insecticide resistance is unclear, as this domain is outside the insecticide binding domain. However, Perry et al. (2008) described insecticide resistance mutations in this domain in the structurally similar nicotinic acetylcholine receptor of Drosophila melanogaster [33]. On the other hand, no significant Tajima´s D values were detected for this gene which might indicate the absence of selection. All non-rare mutations were principally found in South Africa, the Iberian Peninsula, the United Kingdom, or Argentina. Therefore, potential, significant target-site resistance against organochlorine, pyrazole, meta-diamide and avermectin insecticides in A. mellifera may be geographically restricted to those regions or others unrepresented or underrepresented in this study.

The ryanodine receptor had a comparable number of variant alleles per mutation but a higher number of missense mutations per amino acid than the housekeeping genes. This indicates the presence of a large number of rare mutations, further confirmed by a relatively high nucleotide diversity compared to other target sites. Besides the numerous rare mutations, 28 non-rare mutations have been identified. Only six of the 28 non-rare mutations had an FST above 0.9. The exact binding site for diamides, the insecticides that target this receptor, has not been reported. However, fourteen of the non-rare mutations that were identified in this study are located in or close to previously described resistance mutations [25, 76, 77]. Therefore, we suggest that the ryanodine receptor has potential for diamide resistance mutations, although molecular and modelling studies are needed to determine the exact effect of the identified mutations. While these non-rare mutations were not confined to one particular region, Brazil and Sweden harboured the most non-rare mutations, and the number of variant alleles per sample was highest in Oceania, the UK, and the Iberian Peninsula. Three of the six non-rare mutations with FST > 0.9 also had FST values exceeding 0.9 in Portugal. In contrast, the Middle East, Central Africa and South Africa had low diversity for this receptor.

The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor comprises eleven subunits, which display variable genetic diversity. Subunits α2, α9, and β1 had a high number of rare mutations compared to the household genes. Subunit α2 also had a relatively high nucleotide diversity compared to other subunits. In contrast, subunits α3 and α8 had very few mutations, but these occurred at relatively higher frequencies. Both groups can be considered conserved, albeit in different ways. Furthermore, subunits α5, α6, and β2 had the most non-rare mutations and can be considered the least conserved subunits.

Spinosyn insecticides target the homomeric α6 subunit [37, 78]. Twelve non-rare mutations were described in this subunit, all located in the N-terminal domain. This domain is neither part of the insecticide binding domain nor in the proximity of previously described spinosyn resistance mutations [27, 34, 37]. One mutation introduces a premature stop codon at amino acid position 36, resulting in a truncated protein of 388 amino acids instead of the full-length 522 amino acids. This mutation represents a strong candidate resistance variant despite the lack of a significant Tajima´s D value. However, it is expected to incur a fitness cost, as part of the ligand-binding domain is lost [27, 36, 38–43]. This mutation was detected in populations from Saudi Arabia (VAF 57%), Madagascar (36%), Yemen (33%), South Africa (21%), Syria (17%), Kenya (5%), A. m. capensis/scutellata (78%), A. m. unicolor (31%), A. m. jemenitica (17%), A. m. syriaca (14%), and A. m. capensis (6%). In vivo exposure studies in these regions are needed to confirm the physiological impact of this variant.

Neonicotinoid insecticides seem to target subunits α1, α2, α3, α8, and β1, while sulfoxaflor and flupyradifurone, used as replacements for neonicotinoids, mainly target α3 and β1 [78]. Only one non-rare mutation was identified in the ligand-binding domain, which also serves as the insecticide-binding domain, of these subunits [12]. However, resistance to neonicotinoids has also been associated with mutations described in the transmembrane domain and the intracellular linker between the third and fourth transmembrane domains [33]. Fourteen non-rare mutations were found in these domains of the targeted subunits. Therefore, while neonicotinoid resistance mutations appear to be rare within the insecticide binding domain, our data suggest that potential resistance mutations may exist outside of it. Mexico and Brazil harboured the highest number of non-rare mutations in the previously described subunits and domains, while the number of variant alleles per sample was highest in the UK and the Iberian Peninsula. In contrast, Asia, East Africa, and Italy had the lowest number of non-rare mutations. Furthermore, Italy and Scandinavia exhibited the lowest number of variant alleles per sample.

Another potential mechanism for neonicotinoid resistance mutations may involve the α9 and β2 subunits, which are bee-specific and lack homologs in other insect species [79]. The role of these subunits in insecticide resistance has not yet been elucidated. However, the β2 subunit harbours eleven non-rare mutations, all located in the domains associated with insecticide resistance. If this subunit is indeed targeted by insecticides, these mutations could potentially influence resistance. While the South American countries and Algeria had the highest number of non-rare mutations, Portugal, Spain, Egypt and Yemen had the highest number of variant alleles per sample. In contrast, genetic diversity was lowest in North America, Central Europe and Northern Europe.

Acetylcholine esterase 2 harboured a high number of missense mutations per amino acid and a relatively high number of variant alleles per sample, indicating that this target site is less conserved than most other insecticide target sites. Nineteen non-rare mutations were found in acetylcholine esterase 2. Three of these are noteworthy because they introduce indels within or near the ligand and insecticide binding site [30]. These mutations may affect insecticide binding, potentially altering the sensitivity of the target site. However, they could also affect or impair the normal functioning of the target site, possibly incurring a fitness cost [27, 36, 38–43]. These mutations were primarily found in the Middle East, Africa and South America, although one was also detected in the UK with a VAF of 5%. The effects of other mutations on insecticide resistance are unclear, as they are located outside the insecticide-binding domain. It should be noted that there is a mismatch between the RefSeq information and the genomic annotation in Amel_HAv3.1 for a part of this gene. The annotations in this study are based on the genomic annotation in Amel_HAv3.1. Fifteen out of 19 non-rare mutations were found in the mismatched part. Therefore, these described variants should be treated with caution.

The octopamine receptor β2 had a high number of non-synonymous mutations per amino acid and the highest number of variant alleles per non-synonymous mutation, indicating that this receptor is less conserved than the other insecticide target site genes and housekeeping genes. This receptor has four isoforms that are identical for the first 408 amino acids but differ in their C-terminal domain, which varies in length from five to thirty amino acids. Ten non-rare mutations were found in the shared domain, of which five are located within the same functional domain or within five amino acids of previously described amitraz resistance mutations [26, 29, 35, 73]. A nonsense mutation at amino acid 332 is likely to have the strongest impact on insecticide resistance, as it results in a non-functional receptor. This mutation was found in a subset of A. m. scutellata in South Africa. The exact impact of the other mutations on insecticide resistance requires further study but the shared region of the octopamine receptor shows potential for insecticide resistance. Non-rare mutations in the shared domain are nearly absent in North America, Europe, and the Middle East, except in Germany, Poland and Turkey.

Interestingly, 13 of the non-rare mutations found in the octopamine receptor were located in the splicing-specific C-terminal exons, even though this region only comprises a small portion of the receptor. These 13 mutations result in 12 variant isoforms. Isoforms X1 and X2 each have one variant form, while isoform X3 has ten variant isoforms. The effect of these mutations on insecticide resistance is unclear. However, the C-terminal contains important signalling sequences that regulate the interactions with intracellular co-factors [80, 81]. The highest number of non-rare mutations was observed in South America and Kenya, while they were nearly absent in the Middle East. The UK, Kenya and New Zealand had the highest number of variant alleles per sample. Furthermore, Kenya was an outlier in nucleotide diversity for this gene. Based on our data, the previously described differences in amitraz synergy among three North American stocks are probably not caused by target-site resistance, as both the Russian and Wooten stocks have the same three non-rare mutations with similar allele frequencies [47]. However, it is possible that these stocks differ in the isoform ratios of X3B1, X3B4 and X3G.

All of the insecticide target sites play a role in important primary functions, such as thermogenesis, locomotion, social interaction, learning, foraging, and hygienic behaviour [12, 23, 50, 53–56, 82–97]. The mutations described in this study might be driven both by selection for insecticide resistance, selection for their primary physiological functions and even by neutral processes such as genetic drift. Therefore, some of the mutations identified might impact the target site's primary function. For example, ten non-rare mutations were identified in the octopamine receptor β2, all of which had high variant allele frequencies in A. m. monticola, a subspecies native to the Kenyan highlands. This Kenyan diversity is also observed in our nucleotide diversity data. Wallberg et al. (2017) reported that the octopamine receptor β2 is located in a genomic region that is associated with adaptation to high altitude in this subspecies [50]. Therefore, some of the identified mutations may contribute to adaptation to high altitude. Furthermore, according to Saelao et al. (2020), the octopamine receptor β2 is under selection in North American stocks selectively bred for heightened hygienic behaviour. In our study, three non-rare mutations were identified in these stocks, which could potentially be involved in hygienic behaviour and thus contribute to resistance to V. destructor [98]. However, selection for insecticide resistance and primary physiological functions can be at odds, potentially resulting in a fitness cost [27, 36, 38–43]. Several of the non-rare mutations identified here may also carry such costs: for example, the nonsense mutations in the GABA receptor, nAChRα6 and the octopamine receptor β2 or the three indels in the ligand binding domain of AChE2.

Genetic diversity varied geographically, depending on the target site and functional domain. South American countries generally harboured a high number of non-rare mutations, both overall and within insecticide resistance-related regions of the GABA receptor, nAChR, AChE2 and the octopamine receptor. Furthermore, Brazil and Colombia had a significantly higher than average nucleotide diversity. This pattern can be explained by the invasion of Africanized bees and admixture with European lineages [99–103]. Our results support this, as the majority of non-rare mutations found in South America seem to have European or African origins. However, some mutations are unique to South America and are rare or absent on other continents.

Aside from the South American countries, Algeria exhibited the highest number of non-rare mutations, particularly in A. m. intermissa, as well as higher than average nucleotide diversity. Evidence suggests that large-scale queen imports from Europe have not occurred in Algeria, contributing to a unique genetic signature [104, 105]. Our results support this, as 22 out of 35 non-rare mutations identified in Algeria are rare or absent in European populations. Furthermore, 11 of these mutations are unique to Algeria. However, only one non-rare mutation had an FST higher than 0.9, indicating that these Algeria specific variants have a low frequency. This highlights the potential of Algerian honey bee populations as a valuable source of unique genetic variants and diversity.

Turkey, Austria, Syria and Saudi Arabia had the lowest number of non-rare mutations. Three of these countries are located in the Middle East, potentially indicating lower genetic diversity in this region. However, they also have the lowest sample sizes in our dataset, suggesting that the observed pattern may be due to under-sampling rather than true genetic differences. Interestingly, Syria and Saudi Arabia exhibited a relatively high number of non-rare mutations with FST values above 0.9, indicating that the few mutations observed in these regions are highly differentiated and largely region-specific. Further genetic screening in these countries is needed to clarify this.

The UK, Portugal, Spain and A. m. iberiensis showed a high number of variant alleles per sample across all target sites, including insecticide resistance-related regions of the GABA receptor, ryanodine receptor and nAChR. While these countries do not necessarily harbour the highest number of non-rare mutations, the mutations present occur at high(er) frequencies and tend to be unique to their region, given the relatively high number of non-rare mutations with FST values above 0.9 in Portugal and Spain compared to other European countries. In some cases, certain variant alleles are fully fixed within the population. In the UK, 29 of 79 samples originated from conservatories on Colonsay and the Isle of Man, which maintain pure A. m. mellifera lineages, while 45 samples were collected from the Edinburgh region, where admixture between A. m. mellifera and C-lineage subspecies has been reported [106–109]. In Portugal and Spain, the dominant subspecies is A. m. iberiensis, which has limited introgression with other lineages and thus retains high genetic integrity [109, 110]. Both A. m. mellifera and A. m. iberiensis belong to the M-lineage of honeybees, suggesting that this lineage has accumulated insecticide target-site mutations that are absent or rarer in other lineages. These findings highlight the M-lineage as a genetically distinct group with an interesting profile of target-site variants.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We found substantial heterogeneity in rare mutations across the insecticide target sites of A. mellifera. In total, 157 non-rare mutations were identified. Known insecticide resistance mutations reported in literature for other insect species are rare in A. mellifera and likely occur only at low frequencies in specific populations. Target site resistance in the glutamate receptor and sodium channel para is probably rare. In contrast, the GABA receptor Rdl, ryanodine receptor, acetylcholine esterase 2, octopamine β2 and nAChR have the potential to harbour insecticide resistance mutations. However, we did not detect a significant relationship between pesticide use and genetic diversity at these target sites, probably because total pesticide use is an imprecise proxy for insecticide exposure. Nor did we detect significant signals of selection. To better understand the functional consequences of the observed mutations, further in vivo and ex vivo mutational and modelling studies are warranted. Finally, it is important to note that all insecticide target site genes have important primary biological functions, and local adaptation, rather than insecticide pressure alone, may explain much of the genetic diversity observed in this study.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The Sequence Read Archive of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) was accessed on 01/06/2024 [51, 52]. All A. mellifera whole genome sequences (WGS) sequenced with Illumina technology were downloaded in fastq format using SRA-Tools 3.03.3 (https://github.com/ncbi/sra-tools). The final dataset consisted of 4897 unique samples from 54 countries (Tables S59, S60). We defined subspecies according to formally recognised taxonomic classifications [111]. Samples labelled as North American feral, Kona, Russian, Minnesota Hygienic, Hilo, Wooten, Koehnen, Buckfast, and Dongbei bees are not distinct, formally recognised subspecies; therefore, these were classified as populations rather than subspecies. Additionally, some populations included in this study represent admixtures of multiple subspecies (e.g., European hybrid, ligustica/carnica, and capensis/scutellata), and were treated as populations accordingly. A visual representation of the regions and populations covered by the dataset can be found in Figs. 1, 2, 3 and 4. Data from sequencing projects PRJEB16533, PRJEB34590, PRJEB39369, PRJEB43906, PRJEB56749, PRJNA1044268, PRJNA1083455, PRJNA188271, PRJNA216922, PRJNA230767, PRJNA237819, PRJNA252997, PRJNA277772, PRJNA287001, PRJNA292680, PRJNA294105, PRJNA301648, PRJNA306271, PRJNA324081, PRJNA350769, PRJNA357367, PRJNA363032, PRJNA381313, PRJNA385500, PRJNA418015, PRJNA454902, PRJNA471592, PRJNA473430, PRJNA478213, PRJNA481428, PRJNA496560, PRJNA507348, PRJNA507349, PRJNA509410, PRJNA516678, PRJNA521424, PRJNA522435, PRJNA52851, PRJNA578233, PRJNA592197, PRJNA592273, PRJNA596071, PRJNA605407, PRJNA607895, PRJNA622776, PRJNA642095, PRJNA666033, PRJNA688214, PRJNA689474, PRJNA695790, PRJNA729035, PRJNA732718, PRJNA799756, PRJNA824063, PRJNA892909, PRJNA893245, PRJNA936859, PRJNA957323 and PRJNA981429 was used ([50–64], S59). This dataset is comprised of pooled samples and samples from individual worker bees and drones.

All samples were aligned to the A. mellifera reference genome (Amel_HAv3.1) using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner 0.7.17 [112]. The aligned sequences were then converted to the bam format, sorted and PCR duplicates were marked with Sambamba 1.0.1 [113]. Freebayes 1.3.5 was used to perform a joint variant-calling against Amel_HAv3.1 on the exons of 17 insecticide target site genes selected from literature and four housekeeping genes (Table 1) [114, 115]. The housekeeping genes included in this study were selected based on their common use in quantitative PCR experiments [115]. These housekeeping genes are expected to be evolutionarily conserved due to their essential biological functions and were included to provide a comparative baseline. To account for pooled samples in the dataset, the pooled continuous option of Freebayes was used with a minimum variant allele frequency of 0.1 and a minimum variant allele count of two within a single sample. Accordingly, a pooled sample was classified as heterozygous if ≥ 10% of alleles were variant and as homozygous variant if ≥ 90% were variant; in all cases, a minimum of two variant alleles was required to reduce the impact of sequencing errors. Allele frequencies within pooled samples were not further investigated. Despite not explicitly accounting for ploidy during variant calling, quality control analyses indicated that erroneous heterozygous calls in haploid samples were infrequent, averaging 0.1% across all non-synonymous SNPs.

All variants were left-aligned and normalised with BCFtools 1.12 [116]. The variants were then filtered with VCFtools 0.1.16 for a minimum allele count of 3, a minimum phred-scaled quality of 30, a minimum mean coverage depth of 10, a maximum missingness of 0.5 and a minimal coverage depth of 5 per sample [117].

The functional state of the variants (synonymous, non-synonymous, indel, etc.) was obtained with the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor 111 [118]. RefSeq information for AChE2, Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor annotations were manually adjusted based on the A. mellifera reference genome (Amel_HAv3.1) for this specific gene. Furthermore, the variants were annotated with geographical and subspecies data using Plink 1.90b7.2, VCFtools 0.1.16 and BCFtools 1.12 [116, 117, 119]. Finally, automatic UniProt annotations were used to map the structural location of the variants within the proteins. The N-terminal region was defined as everything before the first functional region, while the C-terminal region is everything after the last functional region. The insecticide binding domain was defined based on literature [12, 22, 23, 26, 28–31, 34–38, 41, 65–71, 73]. Annotations for the amino acid position and protein size were based on the largest reference protein possible for that position or gene.

We aligned the A. mellifera protein sequences with homologous protein sequences from organisms described in the literature using BLAST in order to identify corresponding residues and positions to known insecticide mutations [22, 23, 26, 28–31, 35–38, 41, 73, 120]. Countries and subspecies with fewer than five samples were excluded from further calculations. Samples lacking an assigned subspecies or population were excluded from all subspecies/population based analysis. The criteria for the distinction between rare and non-rare mutations were two-fold: the local, in at least one country or subspecies, variant allele frequency (VAF) had to be higher than or equal to 5%, and the local variant allele count (VAC) had to be higher than 2 [57]. The VAC criterion was introduced to reduce false-positive results in countries with low sample sizes. This criterion was applied uniformly across all populations regardless of specific coverage depth of individual pools. Geographical and subspecies variant allele counts were normalised by subtracting the average variant allele count of the country or population in RpL8, RpL32 and actin, adjusted for the relative difference in gene size. Due to the varied backgrounds, sample sizes and ploidy, the variant allele frequency is an estimation of the real allele frequencies.

Pairwise FST was calculated for each country and subspecies with PLINK 1.90b7.2 [119]. Tajima D and nucleotide diversity were estimated using custom scripts developed in R 4.2.1 (R Core Team, 2022. https://www.R-project.org) [121, 122].

All statistical tests were performed in R 4.2.1 (R Core Team, 2022. https://www.R-project.org). An ANOVA type III test was used to determine the significance of the predictor variables. Average pesticide use between 1990 and 2021 was based on data from the FAO [1]. Pairwise comparisons were derived with Tukey's Honest Significant Difference (HSD). In addition, estimated marginal means were contrasted against the grand mean to evaluate whether the Tajima D in each country differed from the overall average.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: A list of all non-synonymous mutations and non-rare mutations can be found in supplementary file 1. A list of all public WGS sequences used with their SRA annotations and accessions (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra) can be found in supplementary file 59. All data to make the figures can be found in supplementary file 60. All software used in the materials is open source. All scripts used in this paper are available in the supplementary files. At a later date, these will be made available on the Zenodo repository of the Better-B consortium.
